title: Early life experiences

draft.title: Early life experiences
card: A child's early experiences can shape health and development well into adult life. The effects can last for decades.
a warm, responsive caregiver who comforts a child and talks and plays with them supports healthy brain growth and emotional security.
a child needs enough healthy food for growth. Poor nutrition early on can affect growth and learning and can raise the risk of health problems later.
ongoing stress in early life, such as neglect or violence at home, can affect how the brain develops. This can affect learning, behaviour and health later.
draft.remember: Care, nutrition and stress in the early years can shape a person's health long into adulthood.

a.q: Why do early life experiences matter so much for a person's health?
opts: Their effects can last for decades into adult life
They only matter until the child starts school
They decide a person's health with no later change
They affect physical growth but not learning or behaviour
a.why: The card says early care, nutrition and stress can shape health for decades. The option about deciding health with no later change is tempting, but the card says they shape health, not that they fix it.
a.clue: Think about how long the effects can last.

b.q: Lena was cared for by warm, responsive adults and ate well in her first years. Her cousin Jack lived with ongoing stress and neglect. Which is the best prediction?
opts: Lena is more likely to have better health and learning later
Jack will certainly have poor health as an adult
Lena and Jack will have the same health outcomes later
Lena's good nutrition will matter, but her care will not
b.why: Good care and nutrition support healthy development, so Lena is more likely to have better outcomes. The statement that Jack will certainly have poor health is tempting, but early stress can affect health, not fix it.
b.clue: Early experiences make outcomes more or less likely, not certain.

a.best: Their effects can last for decades into adult life

b.best: Lena is more likely to have better health and learning later

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('can'). Every distractor uses an absolute ('not', 'no later change', 'only'), so a test-wise student can pick it without knowing the idea.
The clue 'Think about how long the effects can last' points straight at the option about effects lasting for decades, and that option repeats the card's wording almost word for word.
The right option is the only one with a probability qualifier ('more likely'). The others are absolutes ('will not', 'the same', 'certainly'), so it stands out.
The clue 'make outcomes more or less likely, not certain' gives the answer away by naming the 'more likely' wording of the right option.

a.q: Mei had poor nutrition as a toddler. How far into her life can this affect her health?
opts: Through her first year of life
a.why: Poor nutrition early on can raise the risk of health problems later, and early effects can last for decades, well into adult life. Ending at puberty is tempting, but the effects of early life can reach well past the teenage years.
a.clue: Look at what the card says about health problems later on.

b.q: Lena had warm, responsive care and ate well in her first years. Her cousin Jack lived with ongoing stress and neglect. Which prediction fits best?
opts: Jack is more likely to have health and learning problems
Both are equally likely to have problems, as stress fades
Lena is more likely to have problems, having faced no stress
Lena is more likely to have problems, as care spoils children
b.why: Ongoing stress and neglect can affect brain development, which can affect learning and health later, so Jack faces the higher risk. The idea that stress simply fades is tempting, but early effects can last for decades.
b.clue: Which child had the experiences linked to later problems?
